passages.title: How I learnt Portuguese
passages.text:
Learning a new language as an adult can feel impossible. Three years ago I moved to Lisbon for work without knowing a single word of Portuguese. Today I can chat comfortably with my neighbours and even argue with the plumber. Here is what worked for me.

First, I stopped trying to study for hours at the weekend. (1) ______ Instead, I spent twenty minutes on Portuguese every single day, usually on the bus to work. Short, regular practice turned out to be far more effective than long, tiring sessions.

Second, I learnt the words I actually needed. Textbooks often begin with colours and animals, but I needed to buy bread, pay bills and ask for directions. (2) ______ That list became my first vocabulary book, and because I was using the words every day, I remembered them easily.

My third tip is to accept that you will make mistakes. For months I was so worried about saying something wrong that I hardly spoke at all. (3) ______ She told me that people would be pleased I was trying, and she was right. Most people I met were patient and helpful, and some even corrected me in a friendly way.

It also helps to bring the language into your free time. I changed the language on my phone to Portuguese and started watching films with Portuguese subtitles. (4) ______ After a while, though, I found I could follow a whole film without stopping it once.

Finally, find a reason to speak that has nothing to do with lessons. I joined a local running club, where nobody spoke English. (5) ______ Now some of those runners are my closest friends, and I no longer think about which language I'm speaking.

Learning a language takes time, and there is no magic method. But if you practise a little every day and don't give up, you will be surprised how far you can go.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (1)?
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.
F) At first this was very frustrating, as I had to pause every few minutes to look up words.
G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.
questions.explanation: The writer 'stopped trying to study for hours at the weekend'; the sentence about ending up 'tired and bored' and forgetting everything 'by Monday' gives the reason, and 'Instead, I spent twenty minutes... every single day' follows naturally. The sentence about preferring 'a grammar book on Sunday afternoons' is also about weekend study, but it contradicts the writer's decision to stop.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (2)?
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.
F) At first this was very frustrating, as I had to pause every few minutes to look up words.
G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.
questions.explanation: The writer needed words for everyday tasks, not colours and animals, 'So I made a list of every phrase I needed'. The next sentence begins 'That list became my first vocabulary book', which refers back to this list. No other sentence mentions a list.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (3)?
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.

G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.
questions.explanation: The writer 'hardly spoke at all', so Rosa 'noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice'. The next sentence, 'She told me that people would be pleased I was trying', refers to Rosa and repeats her advice. No other sentence introduces a woman who could be 'she'.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (4)?
options: A) Then my landlady, Rosa, noticed how quiet I was and gave me some advice.
B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.
C) In the beginning I could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but gradually we started chatting on the long runs.
D) I always ended up tired and bored, and by Monday I had forgotten most of what I had learnt.
E) This is why I still prefer to study with a grammar book on Sunday afternoons.
F) At first this was very frustrating, as I had to pause every few minutes to look up words.
G) So I made a list of every phrase I needed during the week and asked a colleague to translate it.
H) Luckily, everyone there spoke excellent English, so I never felt lost.
questions.explanation: 'This' refers to watching films with Portuguese subtitles, which was 'very frustrating' because the writer had 'to pause every few minutes'. The next sentence contrasts with it: 'After a while, though, I found I could follow a whole film without stopping it once.' The sentence about being 'tired and bored' does not fit, because it talks about forgetting things 'by Monday', which only makes sense after weekend study.

B) Of course, my friends back home were sure I would never manage to learn such a difficult language.

questions.explanation: In the running club 'nobody spoke English', so at first the writer 'could only say 'hello' and 'well done', but 'gradually we started chatting on the long runs'. This leads to 'Now some of those runners are my closest friends'. The sentence saying 'everyone there spoke excellent English' contradicts the text.
